name: CCW rotation (counterclockwise bimax rotation)

card.summary: A jaw-surgery technique in which the upper and lower jaw are moved together and rotated counterclockwise to bring the chin forward and give a longer, more defined jawline and lower face.
card.note: Major orthognathic surgery with weeks of recovery and risks including nerve numbness and infection.

quick.overview:
Counterclockwise (CCW) rotation is a way of planning bimaxillary jaw surgery. The maxilla and mandible are repositioned as a unit and tilted so the front of the bite moves up and the chin moves forward and up, rather than simply sliding the jaws straight forward.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a route to a more projected chin, a sharper jaw angle and a more open facial profile for people with recessed or vertically long lower faces. Surgical literature studies it for skeletal Class II corrections and for airway enlargement in sleep apnea.
quick.how: The procedure is planned by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon with an orthodontist, usually with braces before surgery, 3D planning, and upper (Le Fort I) and lower (sagittal split) jaw osteotomies, sometimes with a chin procedure. Community members also discuss non-surgical approaches such as mouthguards, posture and growth-phase habits, which are anecdotal.
quick.risks: Orthognathic surgery involves general anaesthesia, swelling, a period on a soft or liquid diet, possible nerve numbness, infection and relapse of the jaw position. Reviews of mandibular CCW advancement note that studies are mostly retrospective case series. Candidacy depends on the individual anatomy and is decided with a surgeon.

lead: Counterclockwise (CCW) rotation is a way of planning double-jaw (bimaxillary) orthognathic surgery in which the upper and lower jaws are moved as one unit, the maxillomandibular complex, and tilted counterclockwise when viewed from the patient's right side. The front of the bite plane rises and the chin moves forward and up, which shortens the vertical height of the lower face and increases chin projection. Surgeons describe it within the family of maxillomandibular advancement operations. [1][2]

The appeal for appearance is that one planned movement changes several features together: a recessed chin comes forward, a steep jaw plane flattens, and the profile reads as more projected and open. Patients with long, downward-growing or recessed lower faces are the typical candidates in forum discussion, and surgeons describe the same pattern as a low-occlusal-plane, high mandibular-plane configuration. In looksmaxxing communities the term is used both for the surgical procedure and, more loosely, for a hoped-for natural change in jaw angle. [3][4][11]

Published research on CCW rotation concentrates on airway enlargement in obstructive sleep apnea, skeletal stability after mandibular advancement, and the role of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) in relapse. Aesthetic outcomes appear mainly in case reports and soft-tissue comparison studies. [1][2][8][11][12][13]

paras: Orthognathic surgery corrects jaw and lower-face problems involving structure, bite, airway and appearance. Typical procedures include the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) for the lower jaw, a Le Fort I osteotomy for the upper jaw and genioplasty for the chin. [5]

CCW rotation is a way of combining these cuts. The jaws are advanced and the occlusal plane (the plane along which the teeth meet) is tilted so that its front end rises relative to the back, changing chin position and jaw-angle appearance more than a straight advancement would. The opposite movement, clockwise rotation, lowers the front of the plane and is used for different problems such as certain Class III and open-bite cases. [1][11][12]

Surgeons usually plan the movement with an orthodontist, using lateral cephalometric X-rays, CT or CBCT imaging and increasingly three-dimensional virtual planning. The amount of rotation is set by the target bite and facial proportions, and the chin may be adjusted separately with a genioplasty, as in a 2018 two-patient case report in which a chin advancement accompanied the jaw movement and the patient's pogonion moved from 4.2 mm to 6.5 mm relative to a reference line. [11]

The Le Fort I maxillary osteotomy on which bimaxillary work builds was developed in its modern surgical-orthodontic form in the 1970s and 1980s, with work by William Bell and colleagues cited in the plastic-surgery literature. [14] The term counterclockwise rotation of the maxillomandibular complex is associated in the literature with the Baylor group around Larry Wolford, whose studies examine rotation with and without TMJ procedures. [13]

In the online looksmaxxing vocabulary the abbreviation 'CCW' became shorthand for a positive jaw rotation, and 'downgrowth' for the opposite pattern. Terms such as 'recessed', 'long face' and 'mouthbreather face' are used for the facial type for which CCW is discussed. Threads proposing it as a reachable outcome have been posted on looksmax.org over several years. [3][4][9][21]

sections.h: Beliefs and claims in the community
paras: Posters present CCW bimax as the surgical answer to a recessed or vertically long lower face and share before-and-after photographs, often alongside infrazygomatic implants and jaw implants in what one thread titled a combined 'guide'. [9][21]

A second strand concerns a natural CCW rotation. Some users ask whether mouthguards, belt-pulling or chewing exercises can tilt the jaws, and others describe puberty-phase habits and growth-related approaches aimed at younger users still growing. Replies in these threads range from enthusiastic personal reports to the statement that such methods matter little after early childhood. [6][10][16][17][18][22][23]

A third strand concerns candidacy: whether it is possible at 19, how a short ramus (the vertical part of the lower jaw) limits the movement, and how asymmetry is handled. Some threads from teenagers also ask about combining surgery with growth-hormone approaches, which are discussed in the community but are outside the surgical literature on CCW. [7][19][20][3]

A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis found that maxillomandibular advancement with CCW rotation produced significant increases in total upper-airway volume and minimum axial area on CT. [1] A 2015 meta-analysis found large improvements in the apnea-hypopnea index and lowest oxygen saturation after maxillomandibular advancement with or without CCW rotation, although the number of patients was too small to compare techniques for pharyngeal volume. [8]

A 2019 systematic review of mandibular CCW rotational advancement for skeletal Class II deformity covered eight retrospective case series, all using rigid fixation, and examined postoperative skeletal stability. [2] A 2008 comparative study of 72 patients with a mean follow-up of 31 months found that CCW maxillomandibular advancement was stable in patients with healthy TMJs and in those who had simultaneous disc repositioning, whereas patients with displaced discs who had no joint procedure showed relapse. [13]

On soft-tissue appearance, a 2024 study of 37 adults and adolescents with Class III deformities compared clockwise (20) and counterclockwise (17) rotation using 3D imaging at nine months. Chin volume and intergonial width decreased more in the clockwise group, and the authors concluded clockwise rotation narrowed the frontal lower face more in that population. [12] A case report of two Class III patients over two years described stable results and an improved chin-to-lip relationship in the patient treated with a counterclockwise plan. [11]

Further papers study airway volume and nasal breathing after orthognathic surgery and whether operating on the mandible first changes the accuracy of upper-jaw positioning in bimaxillary procedures. [15][25]

Human evidence consists of systematic reviews of surgical cohorts, retrospective series, comparative imaging studies and case reports. No randomized trial comparing the aesthetic outcomes of counterclockwise and non-rotational bimaxillary surgery appears in the cited literature. Reviews note that most stability data are retrospective. [1][2][8][12][13]

General orthognathic risks include bleeding, swelling, infection (reported in up to 7 percent of cases) and nerve injury with facial numbness, which usually recovers within about three months but is occasionally permanent. Initial healing takes 2 to 6 weeks and bone healing a further 2 to 4 months. [5]

Relapse of the jaw position is a recognised topic for CCW advancement specifically, and the 2008 study linked it to untreated TMJ disc displacement. Soft-tissue studies of rotation direction also report changes in chin volume and lower-face width that differ by technique. [2][12][13]

CCW rotation sits in the hardmaxxing tier of the community's vocabulary alongside genioplasty, jaw implants and other surgeries. Threads ask how to obtain it, who qualifies and how to combine it with orthodontics, and a number are posted by users in their mid-teens. Before-and-after threads treat the outcome as a way to reduce the look of downward growth. [3][4][9][21]

Non-surgical 'natural CCW' threads form a parallel track, with posters sharing mouthguard ideas, chewing and pulling routines, and personal progress posts; other users in the same threads reply that such approaches are ineffective after childhood. No published study tests these methods for rotating the jaws. [6][10][16][22][23]

timeline.event: William Bell's Le Fort I maxillary osteotomy technique, later foundational to bimaxillary surgery, is published; cited in later surgical-orthodontic reviews.[14]

A 72-patient study led from Brazil with Larry Wolford reports that counterclockwise maxillomandibular advancement is stable with healthy TMJs or with disc repositioning, and relapses when displaced discs are left untreated.[13]
A meta-analysis reports large improvements in apnea-hypopnea index and oxygen saturation after maxillomandibular advancement with or without CCW rotation.[8]
A systematic review and meta-analysis reports significant upper-airway volume gains after maxillomandibular advancement with CCW rotation.[1]
A case report of two Class III patients details occlusal-plane planning and a two-year stable outcome.[11]
A systematic review of eight retrospective series examines skeletal stability after mandibular CCW rotational advancement for Class II deformity.[2]
A 3D soft-tissue study of 37 Class III patients compares clockwise and counterclockwise rotation at nine months.[12]

lore.intro: CCW rotation is a common term in hardmaxxing threads on looksmax.org, where users discuss surgical and non-surgical routes to it, candidacy by age and jaw anatomy, and how it combines with other procedures. [3][4][9]

claims.claim: Bimax surgery with CCW rotation can transform a recessed or downgrown profile
claims.believers: Posters share before-and-after photos and describe a more projected chin and sharper jaw after bimax with rotation. [4][9][21]
claims.experts: Surgical literature documents airway and skeletal changes after CCW advancement, and a case report describes improved chin position; appearance outcomes are reported mostly in case series and imaging comparisons. [1][2][11]

claims.claim: CCW rotation can be achieved naturally with a mouthguard, chewing or pulling routines
claims.believers: Some users report results from mouthguards, belt-pulling or puberty habits and share personal progress posts. [6][10][16][22]
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing these methods for rotating the jaws, and some forum replies themselves say such methods matter little after early childhood. [23]

claims.claim: Puberty-phase habits and tongue posture can steer growth toward positive rotation
claims.believers: Threads aimed at younger users recommend orthodontic intervention, tongue posture and neck training to support the upper jaw during growth. [18][3]
claims.experts: No trial linking these habits to rotation of the jaws was found in the cited literature; orthodontic treatment during growth is a separate clinical field.

claims.claim: A short ramus limits how much CCW rotation is possible
claims.believers: Users ask whether a short ramus caps the achievable change and how surgeons compensate. [7]
claims.experts: Surgeons plan movement from imaging and may add chin or jaw-angle procedures; the cited reviews examine stability rather than ramus length. [2][5]

claims.claim: CCW bimax also enlarges the airway
claims.believers: Posters describe larger airways and better breathing alongside appearance changes. [9][21]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report increased upper-airway volume and improved sleep-apnea indices after maxillomandibular advancement with CCW rotation. [1][8]

claims.believers: Posters present finished results as permanent.
claims.experts: Stability studies report good stability with healthy TMJs and relapse in patients with untreated disc displacement. [13]
